classification.difficultyReason: Translate the fixed perimeter into adjacent sides summing to 12, systematically enumerate whole-number pairs, and compare their areas to establish both extremes.

content.prompt: Imagine that you have a piece of string exactly 24 cm long. On grid paper, draw some different rectangular shapes that can be made using the entire 24 cm piece of string. You know that each of these rectangles has a perimeter of 24 cm. What is the area of each, in square centimetres? How small can you make the area of a rectangle with whole number side lengths? How large?

spec.description: Authored blank grid supplies the grid-paper drawing space requested by the question; the source supplies no printed grid.
spec.mathematics: Students draw rectangles with perimeter 24 cm, choosing and stating a suitable scale.
spec.answerVisibility: No rectangles, dimensions or answers are supplied.

answer.short:
Whole-number dimensions and areas: $1\times11$: $11\text{ cm}^2$; $2\times10$: $20\text{ cm}^2$; $3\times9$: $27\text{ cm}^2$; $4\times8$: $32\text{ cm}^2$; $5\times7$: $35\text{ cm}^2$; $6\times6$: $36\text{ cm}^2$.

Smallest: $11\text{ cm}^2$. Largest: $36\text{ cm}^2$, a square. Adjacent side lengths add to $12$ cm.
answer.worked:
Opposite sides are equal, so half the perimeter is the sum of two adjacent sides:
$$\begin{align*}L+W&=24\div2\\L+W&=12\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
Draw rectangles with dimensions $1\times11$, $2\times10$, $3\times9$, $4\times8$, $5\times7$ and $6\times6$ cm. Rotating a rectangle gives the same dimensions and area.

Using $A=L\times W$:
$$\begin{align*}A_{1\times11}&=1\times11=11\text{ cm}^2\\A_{2\times10}&=2\times10=20\text{ cm}^2\\A_{3\times9}&=3\times9=27\text{ cm}^2\\A_{4\times8}&=4\times8=32\text{ cm}^2\\A_{5\times7}&=5\times7=35\text{ cm}^2\\A_{6\times6}&=6\times6=36\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$
These are all positive whole-number side pairs adding to $12$. The smallest area is $11\text{ cm}^2$ for $1$ cm by $11$ cm. The largest area is $36\text{ cm}^2$ for the $6$ cm square.

spec.description: Six unfilled rectangles at one common scale, in increasing order of shorter side length. Dimension labels give every whole-number possibility up to rotation.
spec.mathematics: Side pairs (11,1), (10,2), (9,3), (8,4), (7,5), (6,6); every perimeter equals 24 cm.
